html:
An English trading company with a royal charter to the trade of West Africa. It began in 1660 as the Company of Royal Adventurers Trading into Africa, set up by the Stuart family and led by the king's brother James, Duke of York, later James II. It was refounded as the Royal African Company in 1672.

It traded gold, ivory and above all enslaved people, and it shipped more Africans across the Atlantic than any other single organisation in the history of the Atlantic slave trade. Most went to sugar islands such as Barbados and Jamaica. Many were branded with the company's initials. It ran forts on the Gold Coast, with its base at Cape Coast Castle. West African gold struck in its name gave England's guinea coin its name.

Its monopoly was ended in 1698 and private traders took over most of the trade. The company declined and was dissolved in 1752. Its rivals included the Dutch at Elmina.
